title: QAOA for Max-Cut
summary: Max-Cut on a 5-vertex graph with a two-layer QAOA.
objectives: Turn a coloring of a graph into a bit string and the number of cut edges into an energy
Build alternating cost and mixer layers and train their angles
Compare the best ratio of one layer with two on the same graph
mission: Cutting more edges of this 5-vertex graph is a Max-Cut problem, and the circuit has to prepare a state whose expected cut is close to the best one. Build a QAOA circuit from Hadamards, cost layers (IsingZZ on every edge) and mixer layers (RX on every qubit), and optimize the angles until the approximation ratio of the state is above 0.85.

prediction.question: You find the best angles for one layer (p = 1) on this graph, then add a second layer and optimize all four angles again. What can you say about the best achievable ratio?
options: It cannot be lower than before: with both angles of the new layer at 0 the circuit is the p = 1 circuit, so that state is still reachable
It can be lower, because four angles are harder to optimize and the optimum moves
It stays the same, because both layers use the same cost Hamiltonian
prediction.explanation: A layer with γ = β = 0 is the identity, so every p = 1 state is also a p = 2 state and the best ratio cannot drop. The optimizer may fail to find it, but the best achievable value does not fall. It can rise, because the second layer reaches one edge further: on this graph it goes from about 0.82 to about 0.92.

hints: What does one layer do to a qubit and to an edge? The cost part acts on pairs of qubits joined by an edge, the mixer part acts on every qubit.
In layer(gamma, beta), apply qml.IsingZZ(gamma, wires=[i, j]) for each edge (i, j), then qml.RX(2 * beta, wires=wire) on each qubit. One layer is not enough to pass 0.85 on this graph.
Take params with one row (gamma, beta) per layer, so shape (2, 2) for two layers, and train with qml.AdamOptimizer(0.1) for about 80 steps. Append circuit(params) to history after each step.

messages.no_circuit: The QNode circuit(params) is missing: define it so that it returns qml.expval(cost_h).
messages.no_params: The trained angles are missing: store them in the variable params.
messages.wrong_qubits: The graph has 5 vertices, one qubit each, but the circuit has {count} qubits.
messages.forbidden_op: This circuit steps outside QAOA: it uses {names}. Build it from Hadamards, IsingZZ and RX (rotations and CNOTs are accepted too).
messages.no_mixer: There is no mixer (RX) in the circuit, so the cost layers only change phases and the probabilities stay uniform: the ratio stays at {ratio}.
messages.p_too_small: Ratio {ratio}, below {threshold}. A single layer cannot get above that on this graph, whatever the angles: use two cost-and-mixer layers.
messages.low_ratio: Ratio {ratio}, below {threshold}. The circuit has enough layers, so the optimizer is stuck or stopped early: train for more steps or start from different angles.

challenge.mission: The mission needed two layers on a 5-vertex graph, but it does not show how much each layer is worth. A ring is the clean case for that, because its optimum is known: on a ring with more than 2p + 1 vertices the best ratio is 0.75 for p = 1 and 5/6 ≈ 0.833 for p = 2, the first two terms of the pattern (2p + 1)/(2p + 2). Use the 8-vertex ring (ring_edges, vertex 7 joined back to vertex 0, and its cost ring_cost_h) and find angles for both depths, with the mission's conventions: |+⟩ on every qubit, then IsingZZ(γ) on every edge and RX(2β) on every qubit, one row (γ, β) per layer. Store them in angles_p1 (shape (1, 2)) and angles_p2 (shape (2, 2)), and the ratios they reach in ratio_p1 and ratio_p2. The validator simulates the ring itself from your angles and requires a ratio of at least 0.745 for p = 1 and 0.83 for p = 2, and your stored ratios must agree with its own to within 0.005.
hints: How many edges can an 8-ring cut at most? Colors that alternate around the ring answer it, and that number is the denominator of the ratio.

Reuse the mission's circuit on 8 qubits with ring_edges and ring_cost_h. Each cut edge gives −1 to ⟨Z_i Z_j⟩ and each uncut edge +1, so the expected cut is (8 − ⟨H⟩)/2 and the ratio is that divided by the maximum cut.

Train p = 1 and p = 2 separately, with qml.AdamOptimizer(0.1) and about 60 steps each. The p = 2 landscape has poor local optima: when a start ends below the p = 1 ratio, change the seed and keep the best of several runs.

messages.ok: The ring gives a ratio of {r1} with one layer and {r2} with two, so the second layer adds {gain}.
messages.ch_no_angles: The variable {name} is missing: store the trained angles there, one row (γ, β) per layer.
messages.ch_bad_angles: {name} must hold {size} finite numbers, a (γ, β) pair for each of the {p} layer(s). Check its shape: p = 1 is (1, 2) and p = 2 is (2, 2).
messages.ch_no_ratio: {name} is missing or is not a single number: store the ratio your angles reach there.
messages.ch_ratio_mismatch: You stored {name} = {reported}, but the ring with those angles gives {actual}. Check that the expected cut is (8 − ⟨H⟩)/2 over a maximum of 8, and that the angles you stored are the ones you evaluated.
messages.ch_low_p1: With one layer the angles give {r1}, below {t1}. The best single layer reaches 0.75 on a ring, so either the training stopped early or the angles are not the final ones.
messages.ch_p2_below_p1: The two-layer angles give {r2}, lower than the {r1} of one layer. A second layer with γ = β = 0 would reproduce the first, so this is a poor local optimum: start again from other angles and keep the best run.
messages.ch_low_p2: With two layers the angles give {r2}, below {t2}. This is better than one layer but short of the optimum of 5/6: train longer or try more starting angles.
